articles.title: Gerrit Graham, Actor in ‘Phantom of the Paradise,’ Screenwriter and Grateful Dead Collaborator, Dies at 77
articles.summary: Gerrit Graham, an actor, screenwriter and songwriter who co-wrote a song for The Grateful Dead, died on Tuesday in Rhinebeck, N.Y. He was 77. He suffered from lung disease, among other ailments.
body: As a screenwriter, Graham worked on projects including “The Little Mermaid,” “Oliver & Company” and episodes of “The Twilight Zone.” He co-wrote the Disney adaptation of “Prince and The Pauper” alongside his brother, Chris Hubbell. Also a songwriter and lyricist, Graham most notably collaborated with Bob Weir of The Grateful Dead. They co-wrote “Victim or The Crime,” which was recorded by the band for their “Built To Last” album and later by Weir and Rob Wasserman on their 1998 “Live” album.

Graham was born in New York City to parents John and Janet, and the family went on to live in Missouri and Michigan before settling in Chicago. In 1982, he married his wife, Deborah, with whom he had two children. He previously served on the Burger Hill Preservation Society while living in Rhinebeck, N.Y., for the last 30 years of his life after caring for his mother in California.
Graham is survived by his brother, Sam; his sons, Jack and Henry, and their wives, Talia and Joelle; and his four grandchildren, Nolan, Micah, Vera and Joey.

articles.title: Gaza Documentary ‘NAZA’ Sets U.S. Theatrical Release Through Self-Distribution Model
articles.summary: “NAZA,” the acclaimed and controversial documentary about killings in Gaza, has set a distribution rollout for U.S. theaters starting Sept. 30 via an innovative plan that forgoes selling the film to a studio or independent distributor.
body: It’s looking like a busy fall for theatrical releases of documentaries: buzzy nonfiction titles set for October openings include Alex Gibney’s “Musk” on Oct. 9 and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc “You Can See Everything” on Oct. 16.

Directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the two Israeli directors of the Oscar-winning documentary “No Other Land,” “NAZA” won a special jury prize at the recent Venice Film Festival. Its North American premiere is at The New York Film Festival on Sept. 26.
“No Other Land” was released in the U.S. through Cinetic with bookings by Michael Tuckman Media rather than using a traditional distributor.

Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, “NAZA” reveals in detail the systems behind “Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to the synopsis. NAZA is the military acronym used by Israeli intelligence to describe the number of civilians it expects will be killed in an airstrike.

articles.title: TV Operators Power Spain’s Global Breakout as the San Sebastian Film Festival Readies Launch: ‘Spanish Cinema Has Never Been So Powerful’
articles.summary: Over the last year or so, Spain has burst onto the world stage, scoring five Cannes main competition berths — more than any other country in the world outside France — with joint best director winner “La Bola Negra” now prominent in awards season conversations.
body: One reason, Rebordinos says, is the work of Spain’s broadcasters and streamers. This year’s San Sebastián is a case in point. Of pay TV/SVOD services, Movistar Plus, the biggest Spanish operator, has three titles in major sections at San Sebastián: “La Bola Negra,” a Neflix U.S. pickup, “El Castillo” and “5 Minutes More,” and Netflix Spain has one: “After Society.”

A Movistar Plus Original like previous Cannes competition contenders “Sirāt” and “The Beloved,” “La Bola Negra” weaves the travails and legacy of Spain’s gay experience in 1932, Spanish Civil War-torn 1937 and 2017, picking up on four pages in an unfinished novel by revered poet-playwright Federico García Lorca. Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi direct.
“Above all, what we’re trying to do is to bet on the best talent, not on genres or formats but creators with their own voices,” says Movistar Plus director of contents Juan Andrés García Ropero.

articles.title: Brad Pitt Returning for ‘World War Z’ Sequel at Paramount With Edward Berger to Direct
articles.summary: Brad Pitt will officially return to star in Paramount’s long-awaited sequel to “World War Z.” “All Quiet on the Western Front” and “Conclave” helmer Edward Berger, who recently directed Pitt in “The Riders” for A24, has signed on to direct from a script by Dennis Kelly.
body: The “World War Z” update comes amid Pitt’s press tour for his latest Paramount movie, “Heart of the Beast,” in theaters next Friday. The survival thriller, directed by David Ayer, follows a Special Forces officer and his combat dog who, after a devastating plane crash, get stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness. Pitt will then reprise his Oscar-winning role in Netflix’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” directed by Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino. The movie debuts in Imax theaters globally on Nov. 25, then begins streaming on Dec. 23. Next up is “The Rider,” which Pitt and Berger wrapped filming on earlier this year; the movie is currently in post-production.

Pitt is represented by CAA and Brillstein Entertainment Partners; Berger is represented by CAA, Range, Casarotto Ramsay & Associates, and Hanson Jacobson; and Kelly is represented by UTA, Casarotto Ramsay & Associates, and Davis Law Group.

articles.title: Zack Snyder is angling to make another Batman movie. Stranger things have happened
articles.summary: Two Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns. There cannot be too many film-makers who have spent quite so long being told that their version of a superhero universe is over, as Zack…
body: In an interview with Variety to promote his forthcoming film The Last Photograph, Snyder returned to an idea he has been talking about for years: adapting Miller’s famously grim 1986 vision of an ageing Batman coming out of retirement in a dystopian Gotham. “The reason why it’s The Dark Knight Returns, if anyone would ever let me do it outside of the DC Universe since it’s a novel that just happens to have superheroes in it, is if I could do Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, those two books next to each other, to me, represent the complete cycle of the superhero comic book medium,” the film-maker said.

“You can do no more than those two books. Watchmen came at the beginning of the superhero movie phase, so it would be super fitting to have The Dark Knight Returns come now, at what I would say is possibly – I don’t want to call it the twilight, but – we’re down the road of the superhero movie genre, and I think audiences would understand the why of it.”

articles.title: Iranian actor Laleh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speech
articles.summary: Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women of Iran’ An Iranian actress who won the best newcomer award at the Venice film festival has come under…
body: Laleh Marzban last Saturday won the best actress award in the Orizzonti sidebar competition for emerging talent, for her role in Mohsen Gharaei’s Falling House, a film revolving around three generations of women who are incarcerated in their own home by the family’s father.

At the awards gala, Marzban dedicated her prize to “the women of my country who have paid the highest price for even the smallest measure of freedom”. Speaking in Farsi, she added that Iranians were experiencing some of the most difficult days of their lives but should not lose hope.

On Thursday, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution, a conservative-dominated government body appointed by Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement condemning Marzban’s speech as “presenting a one-sided narrative of Iran’s proud society”.

Referring only to “recent statements and behaviour made at the Venice film festival”, it said reducing Iranian women to “the stereotypes desired by western circles is not in line with the awareness-raising mission and social commitment of art”.

articles.title: Tenko and Coronation Street actress Stephanie Cole dies aged 84
articles.summary: She was best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.
body: Actress Stephanie Cole, known for roles in Tenko, Open All Hours and Coronation Street, has died aged 84.
A statement from her agent John Grant, issued on behalf of her family, confirmed the actress had been living with Alzheimer's for several years.
"Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television," the statement read.
"She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama. She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities."

articles.title: Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? review – Jarvis Cocker’s wit and warmth upstage the hits
articles.summary: Wonderful archive footage charts the Sheffield outsiders’ unlikely rise, but the distant camerawork struggles to capture the thrill of their triumphant O2 gigs. In 1978, in the classroom of a comprehensive school in Sheffield, a skinny, shortsighted 15-year-old wrote a mission statement in the back…
body: In 2023, after a hiatus of a decade, his band Pulp started touring again, and last year played to 20,000 people at each of two nights at the O2 in London. This film features concert footage from those gigs in which a still lithe, still-got-it-at-60-odd Jarvis Cocker sings his hit art-pop anthems backed by most of the classic lineup and a 10-piece string section. And interspersed with the concert footage are autobiographical musings, nostalgic archive footage, interviews with Jarvis’s mum and gran, and Cocker narrating the story of how he got from there, almost half a century ago, to here.

The total package, in typical Pulp style, is a mixture of the exuberant and celebratory with the bittersweet and reflective. In voiceover, Cocker says that songs “contain pockets of energy from your past life that’s released again when you perform them”. And hearing them performed in the present, you notice how many of the lyrics were about young people wondering what life would be like when they were older. (“Let’s all meet up in the year 2000/Won’t it be strange when we’re all fully grown?”) Which was another way of them wondering whether they were making the right decisions in the present.

articles.title: Harry Potter and the goblet of no booze
articles.summary: The proposal to allow alcohol and music at the event sparks concerns among people living nearby.
body: Organisers of a Harry Potter-themed event have failed to conjure up a licence to sell booze after the plan was turned down amid residents' complaints - and a politician's swipe that "normal men" would not drink the fare on offer.

Forestry England wanted people to have mulled wine and Irish cream hot chocolate as they made their way around an illuminations trail at Cannock Chase Forest in Staffordshire, set to run from October.
The bid was turned down by Cannock Chase District Council which received more than 75 objections, plus the jibe - during a licensing hearing - from a Reform UK councillor.
The applicant had told the hearing that it would ensure there was no adverse impact for neighbours.

articles.title: Unheard Oasis recordings valued at £1.6m for sale
articles.summary: The hidden tapes have been in the possession of a former sound engineer's family for 20 years.
body: Oasis fans are set for a Wonderwall experience when they get the chance to bid for unheard recordings of the Supersonic boys at their peak.
The archive includes recordings of 63 live shows, soundchecks and more than 100 hours of rehearsals from the band's rise and rise in the 1990s that have been valued at between £1.2m and £1.6m.
The lots, which also include original setlists, tour itineraries, a band-played Epiphone guitar and an Oasis tour parka, will be offered for sale on 3 October in Evesham, Worcestershire.
The collection, known as The Desk Tapes, has been in the possession of Owain Richards for 20 years, after his dad, a former front-of-house sound engineer joined the band's crew during their heyday.

articles.title: ‘The damage was much worse than I had imagined’: the shocking inside story of Salman Rushdie’s survival
articles.summary: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life.
body: Eliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic friend, who told her the man she had married just a year earlier, and who had set off the previous night for a speaking engagement nearly 400 miles away, had been hurt. “What kind of hurt?” she panicked. Turning on the television, she was assaulted by blurry images of chaos on stage as audience members surged to the rescue. Her husband, Sir Salman Rushdie, had been stabbed multiple times and was fighting for his life.

Within days of desperately chartering a plane to fly her to Rushdie’s hospital bedside, not knowing if he was alive or dead, Griffiths – a poet and photographer who works under her full name Rachel Eliza Griffiths – had begun to make a video diary recording his treatment and recovery. “When it had become likely that I was going to survive,” says Rushdie drily, “I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this. By which I meant something very modest: maybe she would take a picture of me on her iPhone every couple of days just to document the recovery, but Eliza had bigger ideas.”

The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life.
